idiom_name: handler/view-model struct as supply half; named html/template fragments that render only their data argument
implementation_notes: Go has no component runtime, so the split materialises exactly at the templating boundary: the supply half is a handler (or a small struct with methods) that queries or computes the data and calls ExecuteTemplate with a value, and the presentational half is a named template fragment that receives that value as its dot and can reach nothing else - `{{template "cart-lines" .Lines}}`. What replaces props is the explicit data argument: a template cannot see package state, so a fragment is renderable from a literal struct in a golden-file test and the same fragment serves several handlers. Use html/template for contextual escaping; the hand-written split is the honest default in Go because the standard library offers no component abstraction, and it is only when a UI library such as gomponents or templ is already in the stack that those become the supply half.
pitfalls: Templates parsed after the first Execute fail, and mutating a shared set while it executes races; parse once at startup and treat the set as read-only.
Passing the *http.Request, a database handle or the whole handler into a fragment invites markup to trigger side effects; pass a small view struct with exactly the fields it prints.
text/template, or template.HTML used to 'make it work', removes contextual escaping and turns the presentational half into an injection point.
